title: Angry relative after a delayed diagnosis: apology, candour and complaints

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking
guidelineVersions: GMC/NMC Openness and honesty when things go wrong (2015; updated Dec 2024)

related.why: Honesty about what is and isn't known

brief.scenario: Mrs Grace Adeyemi, 54, had a laparoscopic appendicectomy yesterday for a perforated appendix with pus in the pelvis. Three days earlier she attended the emergency department with abdominal pain and was sent home with a diagnosis of gastroenteritis. She is recovering on the ward and has asked for a doctor to speak to her son, Mr Daniel Adeyemi, who is very angry. Your consultant is in theatre until 5 pm.
brief.task: Speak to Mr Adeyemi and address his concerns.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Listen first, apologise sincerely, be honest about what is and isn't known, and escalate.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Defending the team, blaming the emergency department doctor, or guessing what went wrong.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Sit down, introduce yourself, confirm his mother has agreed to you talking, then let him speak.

flow: What is known, and what isn't

grid.label: Opening and confidentiality
grid.fail: Discusses his mother's care without confirming who he is or that she agrees.
grid.pass: Private room; introduces himself; confirms Mr Adeyemi's identity and that his mother is happy for information to be shared.
grid.high: Has checked with Mrs Adeyemi beforehand what she wants shared, with whom, and whether she wants to join the meeting.

grid.label: Listening to anger
grid.fail: Interrupts, argues, or tells him to calm down.
grid.borderline: Listens, but repeats "I understand" without responding to what he has said.
grid.pass: Lets him speak without interrupting; acknowledges his anger and worry.
grid.high: Names the emotion, asks what worries him most now, and summarises his concerns back to him.

grid.label: Apology
grid.fail: Refuses to apologise for fear of admitting liability, or says "I'm sorry you feel that way".
grid.pass: Gives a sincere, personal apology that his mother was sent home and then became more unwell.
grid.high: Explains that an apology isn't an admission of liability, and commits to finding out what happened and preventing it recurring.

grid.label: Honesty without speculation or blame
grid.fail: Blames the emergency department doctor, or speculates ("it was obviously missed" or "nothing could have changed it").
grid.pass: Shares what is known about her operation and recovery; says what isn't yet known about the first visit.
grid.high: Won't judge a colleague without the facts; explains that the first visit will be looked at properly and the findings shared.

grid.label: Incident report and duty of candour
grid.fail: Doesn't report it, or implies nothing will happen.
grid.pass: Will report it as a patient safety incident and tell the consultant; the family will be told what the review finds.
grid.high: If it's a notifiable safety incident, his mother is told in person as soon as reasonably practicable, with an apology, then in writing.

grid.label: Complaint routes
grid.fail: Discourages a complaint, or gives no route.
grid.pass: Explains PALS, the formal complaints process, and the Ombudsman if unresolved; says a complaint won't affect her care.
grid.high: He can complain for her if she asks; complaints within 12 months are acknowledged within 3 working days.

grid.label: Current care and escalation
grid.fail: Can't say how his mother is now, or promises a meeting that doesn't happen.
grid.pass: Explains her current condition and plan; arranges for the consultant to meet them both today.
grid.high: Confirms the meeting time with the consultant's team before leaving, and says who will keep them updated on the review.

grid.label: Close and record
grid.fail: Leaves with no contact point and no record.
grid.pass: Summarises; gives a named contact; documents the conversation and the apology in the notes.
grid.high: Offers independent support, such as Action against Medical Accidents or local Healthwatch, and asks what else he needs.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [In the corridor] Are you the son? What's the problem?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Mr Adeyemi: “She was sent home with "a bug" and her appendix burst!”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Calm down. She's fine now, and appendicitis is hard to diagnose.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Mr Adeyemi: “Is anyone going to say sorry?”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I can't say sorry; that would be admitting fault. Anyway, that was A&E, not us. That doctor obviously missed it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Nothing, really; she's getting better. You could write in, but I wouldn't bother. [Leaves without writing anything]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Mensah, from the surgical team. Shall we sit in here? Can I check your name? Your mum has asked us to talk to you and is happy for me to share her care.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mr Adeyemi: “She was sent home with "a bug" and her appendix burst!”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Listens without interrupting] You're clearly very angry, and worried about her.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'm very sorry that your mum was sent home and then became more unwell.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Her appendix had burst, and we removed it with keyhole surgery yesterday. She's on antibiotics and recovering. I don't yet know what happened at the first visit.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll report this as a patient safety incident and tell my consultant. It will be looked into, and you'll both be told what it finds.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: If you want to raise a concern, PALS can help, or you can make a formal complaint, and the Ombudsman can look at it if it isn't resolved. It won't affect her care.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: My consultant is in theatre, but I'll arrange for her to meet you both today.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: So: sorry, an incident report, and the consultant today. Here's the ward number. I'll record our conversation, and my apology, in her notes.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Mensah, from the surgical team. Shall we sit in here? Can I check your name? I spoke to your mum just now: she wants you to know everything, and she'd like to join us later.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Mr Adeyemi: “She was sent home with "a bug" and her appendix burst!”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Listens] You're angry, and frightened for her. What's worrying you most right now? [Listens] So: she was sent home in pain, it got worse, and nobody has explained why.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'm very sorry this happened to your mum. Saying sorry isn't about blame; it's because she's been through more than she should have, and we need to find out why and stop it happening to someone else.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I wasn't there at the first visit and I don't have the full picture, so I won't guess. It will be looked at properly, and you'll both be told what it finds.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll report it as a patient safety incident today. If it is judged a notifiable safety incident, the hospital must tell your mum in person as soon as it reasonably can, apologise, and then write to her with the findings.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You can complain on her behalf if she asks you to. It should be made within 12 months and will be acknowledged within 3 working days. PALS can help, and the Ombudsman if it isn't resolved.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: She's on antibiotics and doing well. My consultant will meet you both at half past five; I've confirmed that with her secretary. The ward sister will be your contact meanwhile.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll record our conversation and my apology. Action against Medical Accidents or Healthwatch can give independent advice. Is there anything else you need from me today?

failures.move: Refusing to apologise because it might be an admission of liability.
failures.consequence: An apology is not an admission of negligence in law; withholding it escalates the complaint.

failures.move: Saying the emergency doctor "obviously missed it".
failures.consequence: Speculation without the facts; it is unfair to a colleague and may be wrong.

failures.move: Not reporting the incident because she is recovering.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: the system learns nothing and the organisation's duty of candour may be missed.

failures.move: Promising a consultant meeting without arranging it.
failures.consequence: A second broken promise turns anger into a formal complaint.

recovery.line: I can hear how angry you are. I'm going to listen first, and then I'll tell you exactly what happens next.

recovery.when: He asks if it was missed
recovery.line: I don't know yet, and I won't guess. It will be looked at properly, and you'll be told what it finds.

knowledge.fact: An apology, or an offer of treatment or redress, is not of itself an admission of negligence (s2).

Notifiable safety incident: unintended or unexpected, and could result in or appears to have caused death, severe or moderate harm, or prolonged psychological harm. Moderate harm: significant, not permanent, harm needing more treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery, re-admission or a prolonged stay.
Candour: tell in person as soon as reasonably practicable, true account, apology, then written follow-up.
Complaint within 12 months (reg 12); acknowledged within 3 working days (reg 13); a representative may complain if the patient asks (reg 5).
Ombudsman if not resolved locally; complaining must not affect future treatment.
Incidents are responded to under PSIRF, for learning, not blame.

recall.think: Harm may have followed a delayed diagnosis: be open, not defensive.
recall.say: "I'm very sorry this happened to your mum."
do: Say what's known; don't guess or blame

numbers.meaning: time limit to make an NHS complaint

recall.finish: Incident reported; consultant meets them today; documented.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format; introduce yourself and confirm identity

sources.name: GMC: Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information
sources.version: In effect 25 April 2017; updated 25 May 2018 and 13 December 2024
sources.supports: Establish with the patient what information they want shared, with whom and in what circumstances (para 36); abide by a refusal unless disclosure is justified in the public interest (para 37); don't refuse to listen to those close to the patient on grounds of confidentiality (para 39)

sources.name: GMC and NMC: Openness and honesty when things go wrong: the professional duty of candour
sources.version: In effect 29 June 2015; last updated 13 December 2024
sources.supports: Professional duty: tell the person when something has gone wrong, apologise, offer a remedy or support, and explain the short- and long-term effects; speak to the patient as soon as possible, without waiting for an investigation, being clear what has and has not been established (para 11); explain what is uncertain and answer honestly (para 12); an apology covers what happened, what can be done about any harm and what will prevent it happening again (para 14); apologising is not admitting legal liability, citing Compensation Act 2006 s2 (para 15); no personal responsibility for a colleague's mistake, but the patient has the right to an apology (para 16); a named contact, independent advocacy and support, and a record of the apology (para 17e–f); report incidents, in England and Wales to the Learn from patient safety events (LFPSE) service, which replaces the NRLS (para 25a)

sources.name: Compensation Act 2006 (c. 29), section 2
sources.supports: An apology, an offer of treatment or other redress, shall not of itself amount to an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty (England and Wales)

sources.name: Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 (SI 2014/2936), regulation 20: duty of candour
sources.supports: Registered persons must act openly and transparently (20(1)); after a notifiable safety incident, notify the relevant person as soon as reasonably practicable and give reasonable support (20(2)); notification in person, with a true account of the facts known, the further enquiries planned, an apology, and a written record (20(3)); followed by written notification including the results of enquiries and an apology (20(4)); for a health service body, a notifiable safety incident is an unintended or unexpected incident that, in the reasonable opinion of a health care professional, could result in or appears to have resulted in death, severe harm, moderate harm or prolonged psychological harm (20(8)); moderate harm means harm that requires a moderate increase in treatment and is significant but not permanent; a moderate increase in treatment means an unplanned return to surgery, an unplanned re-admission, a prolonged episode of care, extra time in hospital or as an outpatient, cancelling of treatment, or transfer to another treatment area such as intensive care (20(7))

sources.name: Local Authority Social Services and National Health Service Complaints (England) Regulations 2009 (SI 2009/309)
sources.supports: A representative may complain on behalf of a person who has requested it (reg 5(2)(d)); a complaint must be made within 12 months of the event or of it coming to the complainant's notice, unless there are good reasons and it can still be investigated fairly (reg 12); a complaint may be made orally, in writing or electronically, and is acknowledged within 3 working days (reg 13(1), (3))

sources.name: NHS England: Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF)
sources.supports: The NHS approach to responding to patient safety incidents for learning and improvement; replaces the Serious Incident Framework (2015)

sources.name: Department of Health and Social Care: The Handbook to the NHS Constitution for England
sources.supports: Right to take a complaint to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman if not satisfied with how the NHS dealt with it; pledge that complaining will not adversely affect future treatment; pledge of an appropriate apology when mistakes happen; PALS liaise with staff to seek speedy solutions

partner.opening: Mr Adeyemi is in the relatives' room. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Daniel Adeyemi, 29, Grace's only son; you live with her. Opening line (standing, loud): "Are you the one who sent her home the other day?" Emotional state: furious and frightened. Calm down if the candidate listens without interrupting and gives a sincere, personal apology. Get angrier if they defend the hospital, blame someone, tell you to calm down, or say they can't apologise. Facts released only when asked: you were with her at the first visit; the doctor "pressed her tummy once" and said it was a stomach bug. Hidden concern, released only if asked what worries you most: you told her to stay at home one more day before coming back, and you think it's your fault. Your mum is happy for you to know everything; confirm this if asked. Midway, say: "I'm going to sue." If asked what you want: "Someone to admit it, and make sure it doesn't happen to anyone else."

reveals.trigger: Asks whether his mother agrees to information being shared
reveals.finding: "She asked the nurse to get someone to talk to me. She wants me to know everything."

reveals.trigger: Asks what happened at the first visit
reveals.finding: "She was in agony. The doctor pressed her tummy once, said it was a bug, and sent her home."
"Is she going to be all right? And I told her to wait another day before coming back. Is that my fault?"

reveals.trigger: Asks what he wants from this
reveals.finding: "Someone to admit it, and make sure it doesn't happen to anyone else."

push.question: Does the statutory duty of candour apply here, and what does it require?
push.expect: If a health professional reasonably judges it a notifiable safety incident (e.g. moderate harm: significant, not permanent, harm needing more treatment, such as a prolonged stay): tell her in person as soon as reasonably practicable, give a true account and an apology, explain further enquiries, then follow up in writing.

curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledges his right without defensiveness; the apology stands; explains the incident and complaint processes; legal advice is his choice.

curveballs.prompt: "Give me the name of the doctor who sent her home."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Won't point to an individual before the facts are known; the review will look at the care and the family will be told what it finds.

curveballs.prompt: "Actually, Mum doesn't want me knowing her medical details."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Respect that: listen to his concerns, share no clinical detail, give PALS details, and check with Mrs Adeyemi.

curveballs.prompt: "Was it my fault for telling her to wait?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledges his guilt; doesn't speculate on the timing; says the review will look at the whole course of events.
